query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If a high-entropy alloy is subjected to simultaneous thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and in-situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) at elevated temperatures under a controlled oxygen environment, then the real-time progression of oxidation and phase transformations can be accurately tracked, revealing both the kinetics of oxide formation and the stability of underlying phases.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized high-entropy alloy with uniform microstructure, prepared for high-temperature assessment.
generation.intervention: Raising the temperature of the alloy up to 1000°C in a controlled oxygen partial pressure while collecting TGA and in-situ XRD data continuously.
generation.conditions: Thermal ramp to 1000°C at a chosen rate (e.g., 10°C/min) in an environment with fixed oxygen partial pressure (e.g., 10−4–10−1 atm of O2).
generation.structural_mediator: Real-time formation and evolution of oxide phases at high temperature, as observed through diffraction patterns.
generation.mechanism: Mass changes from TGA are directly correlated with the appearance or disappearance of diffraction peaks, thereby linking oxidation kinetics to phase evolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: In-situ data will show a measurable mass gain corresponding to oxide-scale growth, concurrently with the emergence of new oxide phases and possible transformations in the metallic lattice.
generation.baseline: Ex-situ measurements after oxidation (post-testing) typically capture only final states and may miss transient phases.
generation.boundary: Results may differ for alloys with varying compositions, pressure ranges, or temperature profiles; the approach may require optimization for very rapid oxidation kinetics or extreme temperatures above 1000°C.
generation.uncertainty: Minor compositional inhomogeneities, variations in sample geometry, and differences in ramping rates may affect oxidation kinetics and phase identification.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel trials on reference and experimental samples. Verify that phases identified by in-situ XRD match post-mortem ex-situ characterizations (e.g., scanning electron microscopy, XRD at room temperature), and that TGA-derived oxidation kinetics align with thickness measurements of any oxide layers. If discrepancies exist beyond experimental uncertainty, the hypothesis is falsified.
measurements: Phase evolution via in-situ XRD patterns recorded at temperature intervals
Post-experiment surface and cross-sectional oxide thickness by microscopy and ex-situ XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If transient phases or oxidation rates differ significantly from TGA and in-situ XRD results when validated by ex-situ methods, or if no new oxide phases are detected as predicted, the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
